title: Ὄνος βαστάζων ἄγαλμα
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 266. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνῳ τις ἐπιθεὶς ἄγαλμα ἤλαυνεν εἰς ἄστυ.
sentences.tr: Onōi tis epitheis agalma ēlaunen eis asty.
sentences.l: Someone, having set an image upon a donkey, was driving him into town.
sentences.n: ἄγαλμα is the image set up for a god and honoured as the god's own. At fable 108 it stands in a sculptor's shop and the corpus calls it a statue; here it is carried in procession and receives obeisance, so 'image'. ἐπιτίθημι puts the load on in the dative.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ συναντώντων προσκυνούντων τὸ ἄγαλμα, ὁ ὄνος ὑπολαβὼν ὅτι αὐτὸν προσκυνοῦσιν, ἀναπτερωθεὶς ὠγκᾶτό τε καὶ οὐκέτι περαιτέρω προϊέναι ἐβούλετο.
sentences.tr: Tōn de synantōntōn proskynountōn to agalma, ho onos hypolabōn hoti auton proskynousin, anapterōtheis ōnkato te kai ouketi peraiterō proienai ebouleto.
sentences.l: And as those who met them were making obeisance to the image, the donkey, supposing that they were making obeisance to him, set aflutter, both brayed and no longer wished to go any further forward.
sentences.i: And when the people they met bowed down before the image, the donkey took it that they were bowing to him, and, all in a flutter, began to bray and would go no further.
sentences.n: προσκυνέω is the bodily act — a bow, or a kiss blown toward the god — not an inward reverence. ἀναπτερόω is to set a creature's feathers up, to make it flutter with excitement. ὠγκᾶτο is the donkey's own verb, to bray; the ass of fable 208 does the same inside the goats' cave.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὁ ὀνηλάτης αἰσθόμενος τὸ γεγονὸς τῷ ῥοπάλῳ αὐτὸν παίων ἔφη· « Ὦ κακὴ κεφαλή, ἔτι καὶ τοῦτο λοιπὸν ἦν ὄνον ὑπ’ ἀνθρώπων προσκυνεῖσθαι. »
sentences.tr: Kai ho onēlatēs aisthomenos to gegonos tōi rhopalōi auton paiōn ephē· « Ō kakē kephalē, eti kai touto loipon ēn onon hyp’ anthrōpōn proskyneisthai. »
sentences.l: And the donkey-driver, having perceived what had happened, striking him with his club, said: « O wicked head, this too was still left — for a donkey to be bowed down to by men. »
sentences.i: And the driver saw what had got into him and beat him with his club, saying: « You wicked creature, so this was all that was still wanting — that a donkey should be bowed down to by men. »
sentences.n: κακὴ κεφαλή, 'wicked head', is standard Greek abuse, the head standing for the whole man; the corpus keeps the literal phrase (as at fable 64 and fable 187). τὸ γεγονός is a perfect participle used as a noun, 'the thing that has come about'. λοιπὸν ἦν with the infinitive is heavy sarcasm: of everything left undone in the world, this was the one remaining.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ τοῖς ἀλλοτρίοις ἀγαθοῖς ἐπαλαζονευόμενοι παρὰ τοῖς εἰδόσιν αὐτοὺς γέλωτα ὀφλισκάνουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi tois allotriois agathois epalazoneuomenoi para tois eidosin autous gelōta ophliskanousin.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who play the braggart on the strength of another's goods incur ridicule among those who know them.
sentences.n: ὀφλισκάνω is a courtroom word — to have a judgement go against one; what these men are sentenced to is laughter (as at fable 121 and fable 208). ἐπαλαζονεύομαι takes the dative of what is boasted of, and here the goods are ἀλλότρια, someone else's.
